lines: Every topic before this one asked which table format to write.
None of them asked who reads it back.
That's new ground: splitting one query's work across a fleet of machines.
Picture a long query, most of the way through, and one machine drops out.
Does the rest of the cluster shrug it off, or does everybody start over?
answer: A dropped machine means a human has to resubmit the entire thing.

lines: One machine plans the whole thing out and hands pieces to the rest.
Those other machines never see the original request.
They just run their piece and pass results along to whoever needs them next.
Here's a trick worth remembering: look at one side of a join first.
Whatever keys show up there are the only keys worth fetching on the other side.
Skip the rest before a single row of it gets read.
Two tables, wildly different sizes, about to be joined.
The engine already knows roughly how big each one is.
Which one does it load into memory to drive the match?
answer: Loading the smaller side into memory is cheaper than loading the large one.

lines: Size wins, and that choice comes straight from counting rows ahead of time.
Take the counts away, though, and the planner goes conservative.
It stops guessing at a smart order and just avoids the obviously dumb one.
There's a second mode built for exactly the failure from a few steps back.
Instead of restarting everything, only the piece that died gets redone.
Everything else that already finished stays put, nothing recomputed.
This engine used to carry a different name entirely.
Its own creators walked away from the company that built it, over who controlled its future.
A trademark fight a year later forced the new name to stick.
The company left behind kept building its own version in parallel.
Years later, that version got a from-scratch engine written in a faster language underneath it.
Same brain on top, a completely different set of hands doing the work.
A planner that survives a dead machine, a filter that skips unneeded data, a size-aware join.
Every one of those ran for real against this chapter's own table.
Next question: what if the engine and the storage were never two separate things?
